body:
The amount of code being written at Anthropic continues to rise exponentially. It is being managed by Scion, their internal replacement for GitHub that is better suited to the scale and style of the operation, which they created with a small team in five months.

This week also saw the release of two supposed frontier model models.

Google has finally given us Gemini 4 Argon, along with a robust safety report. We do not yet know if Argon lives up to its benchmarks or internal hype. I plan to write up the safety report next week, time permitting. If and only if it is good enough or discussed enough we will also have a full report on capabilities.

Meta gave us Muse Wonder, which like Argon has some excellent benchmarks, although they were presented in a way that looked rather sus. There are some reports that it is very good, but again it is too early to know. I will issue a full report if and only if Muse Wonder has capabilities or discussion that seem worthy.

To help me decide and to let people have fun, I have markets on whether I will issue the reports on Argon and Wonder , respectfully.

OpenAI caught an employee planting a bug. How many more spies are out there?

A group used ChatGPT to create a full-chain exploit of Chrome and claimed a 250,000 bounty. Luckily for us it was the good guys this time.

Like most weeks, I covered a lot more. It was only a little over a week ago that OpenAI dumped solutions to hundreds of math problems . Then came news that OpenAI fired three safety researchers , without providing us a good explanation. Once again we went over the fact that arguments about AI consciousness remain highly motivated and at best overconfident . Finally, I emphasized that the safety culture at the labs is broken , which is one of the most important facts about the world.

Today I am flying out to another conference at Lighthaven. I probably posted this from the airport and it won’t include any events from last night, tomorrow’s post will be the monthly and Monday may be from the non-AI queue. This coming week will then be another case of me scrambling to catch up, especially with the model reviews still potentially looming.

- Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Prompting is easy now.

- Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Writing still needs work.

- Huh, Upgrades . Muse Wonder and Gemini 4 Argon.

- On Your Marks. Are you sure the models got that question wrong?

- Choose Your Fighter. Theo is a fan of Haiku 5.5.

- Get My Agent On The Line. Agent retention rates are okay but not great.

- Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. Literary world keeps getting exposed.

- Cyber Lack of Security . A full-chain exploit of Chrome found in six days.

- Spy Versus Spy . OpenAI employee caught planting a physical bug.

- The Internet of AI Things. AIs might soon haunt various devices.

- A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. AI is changing motherhood.

- They Took Our Jobs. Epic Games to have an epic lack of human-written code.

- Introducing. Microsoft-Decision-1 is based on… Qwen 3.5-9B? Really?

- In Other AI News. The State of AI report isn’t what it used to be.

- Massive Fraudulent Distillation. The fight continues.

- Show Me the Money . Anthropic Q3 revenue of 16.8b. Nvidia to buy Reflection.

- Quiet Speculations. There is accounting for taste, given enough data.

- Quickly, There’s No Time. Timelines to RSI keep shrinking, moving into [AI] 2027.

- The Quest for Sane Regulations. UK AISI regains access, CAISSI to White House.

- Chip City. GPUs can be cheaper to buy then to rent by a large margin.

- The Week in Audio. Soares, Lovely, Patel, Wang.

- People Just Say Things.

- The Virtue of Silence. [CENSORED].

- Rhetorical Innovation. The four classes of AI user expertise levels.

- [Artificial Intelligence]. We have met the enemy, and he is everywhere.

- Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. AI as insider risk.

- Backdoor Man. Backdoors, and other things, are easy to insert and hard to remove.

- Cooperative Alignment. Decision theory gives us some arguments for hope.

- People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone. The AI will be smarter than you.

- Other People Are Not As Worried About AI Killing Everyone. They don’t know.

- The Lighter Side. You know what you did.

#### Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Prompting is easy now. As Boris Cherny says, tell the AI what you want to do , how to verify that it did it, and how much effort to spend, and you’re good. I’d add ‘and anything it needs to know.’ Presumably that was implied. Boris prompts on Slack , which means Claude already has a lot of context, enabling shorter prompts.

Do you trust Grok to go use your credit card without pausing for approval?

Elon Musk : To buy stuff, you can just take a picture of your credit card, drop it in the chat and Grok @Bot will scour the Internet for the best deal on the item you want and order it.

[Community note: No that’s not how you upload your CC information.]

The correct maximally allowed error rate on such actions is not zero. It also is not high, and if you are using this blind you likely will have no idea if it is getting the best price or the best item. Then again, did you know before?

How easy is prompting? Pliny shuffled this off to Opus 5.5 with a 200 subscription:

“can you wraite a promtp for a cron job that can run every day thajt will try to find solutions to unsolved ciphers or transltions or math problems or theormes or things of that nature!! every day a new attempt as hard as possible all day without giving ujp and with maximum ceraitvityy, resourcesleflses, andpersticense! dont worry about token spend! and dont forget a bit all caps lots of emojis celebration to notify the uers if we get any intersting or sucsfful confirmd reulsts!!”​

day 1, the legion picked its own target: J.-F. Bouchaudy’s cipher-machine challenges. these are simulations of real vintage machines (Hebern rotor machines, the Kryha, Lorenz, SIGABA), with problems that had been sitting on his solver tables with no solver for months or years.

on the morning of day 2, i was half asleep when my laptop suddenly says, in a robot voice:

“Breakthrough. The Daily Oracle has a confirmed solution.”

then the ALL CAPS emoji flood hits my screen. Hebern 5-rotor Problem 8 then Kryha v2 Problem 5

i emailed the author, Jean-François Bouchaudy, a French cryptography enthusiast who builds these machine simulators and challenges as a labor of love (he told me he started out programming on punch cards ). he checked both solutions and put my name on his solver tables as the first and only solver

This is the correct version of ‘do a breakthrough, make no mistakes.’ It’s that easy.

A thought experiment from Terence Tao :

It seems ethical, in a sane world, to allow volunteers to participate in such trials. If the cocktail passes a Phase 3 trial, then we should conclude that it works. No, I absolutely would not, if I had cancer, demand that there was a human who ‘understood how it works,’ and if the FDA required that I would yell about it a lot. Yes, of course you would also want to model tail risks that might not be showing up and take those risks into account, so I wouldn’t use this lightly, but if the cancer is lethal and otherwise untreatable then why not?

Obviously you would also have to worry about some form of active misalignment, and that this was part of some sort of takeover or similar attempt, at that point, but that is a very different concern than the ones Tao is presumably considering.

Tao instead has the next point be ‘the AI hacked the FDA and the drug both does not work and kills people’ but even if the AI is being malicious for the lulz no one going to do this by hacking the FDA, in the sense that the Phase 3 trial is a physical thing with many artifacts in the world, that is then examined by humans? So we would just notice. And if we didn’t, we’d notice pretty quickly after that. The only real risk is long-latency-only harm, which is already true today and has limited downside if you are treating otherwise deadly cancers.

Talk and write to people whose expertise lies elsewhere:

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): By the way, in my experience contractors of all sorts have adopted AI for text-based communications and it has substantially improved coordination on home renovation projects

#### Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

Remember that, no matter how great Opus 5.5 is (and it’s pretty great), how many contributions you make or lines of code you write is not a good measure of productivity.

Ado (Anthropic): The weekend after Opus 5.5 launched I had my most productive coding day of the year (so far).

AI writing now once again lags behind AI math.

Matthew Yglesias : AI cracking unsolvable math problems while being kinda mid at writing is a much-needed W for humanities majors after a rough 21st century.

Paul Graham : Apparently it’s mostly just because they haven’t made much of an effort to train it to write well yet.

Matthew Yglesias : I’ve been reliably informed my work isn’t economically valuable enough to be worth investing time on automating.

Miles Brundage : Mostly just cuz there are like 2 ppl working on it though

Matthew Yglesias : Let us have this

Better AI writing would be highly economically valuable, so my guess is this is mostly not ‘we forgot to put 10 or even 50 guys on it instead of 2.’ You’d have to work a lot harder than that. The alternative hypothesis is ‘you may not like it but this is what peak performance looks like,’ that the people love their Claudeslop and it works, and we would react inherently negatively to AI writing no matter what it sounds like. Sure, it would be better if for those who care it could vary more and be higher Quality, but is that worth the price?

I don’t know. I can see it both ways. My guess is the Claudeslop has short term benefits, but continued use of it accumulates long term costs and fatigue. In general, when faced with such choices, modern capitalism is often myopic and gets in trouble.

Who gets the blame if AI fails ? Opinions differ greatly.

It depends on the situation. There is no universal answer.

Meta’s Muse Wonder exists . It sports excellent benchmarks, with the ‘Full’ version scoring 56 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence, two behind Opus 5.5. However, Muse Spark 1.3 had the same rating there as GPT-6 Sol and was only one point behind Astra and Fable 5.1, and I don’t know of anyone who thinks Muse Spark 1.3 could hang with those other three offerings. Various signs suggest benchmaxxing, including how they chose to display their other benchmarks.

As always, reserve initial judgment, do not read too much into benchmarks and if you think it is worthwhile run your own experiments, including with matching prompts across models, and report back. Due to my trip, if Wonder proves worthy of extended coverage look for that around Wednesday next week.

Gemini 4 Argon is live for Pro and Ultra users , and in the AI Overlay and hopefully by now everywhere Google AI products are served. We now wait to see if it lives up to its claims and hype. If it does, we will have full coverage, again some time later next week.

The tentative plan is to do a full read of their 200+ page safety and security report , the same way I do with Anthropic models, and go from there. I can’t do that every Google and Anthropic release, it would be too much, but this is a big jump for Google.

Claude Dashboards and Claude Motion are now in beta. You can now create various charts and also short animations, with a slightly easier interface than before.

Claude now offers the type “multiagent_20261001 ”. This does what it sounds like.

Google has a new internal model, for now named Gemini 4 Carbon , available inside their internal coding platform Jetski, with claims it is very good.

Hugh Langley : An internal document shows that Google has tested a series of Gemini 4 models, internally named Argon, Barium, and Carbon.

I am highly disappointed if the reason for Argon was alphabetical. Lamest secret coding system ever. If you are going to do elements, be an actual nerd and use the periodic table. I should call it Gemini 4A in protest, but I probably won’t.

Opus 5.5 is the first model to successfully clock Joe Weisenthal identity based on a few pages of an unfinished novel from a few years ago.

Are you sure the model got the eval question wrong?

Alex Tabarrok : We are now at “the fuck” levels.

Nirmalya Kajuri : “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5.

But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, A stra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50 ).”

Last week math. Soon, physics. Then, presumably, chemistry.

I agree with Charbel-Raphael that the marginal value of AI ‘safety’ evals is low . Internal evals still do matter, and it is good to keep tabs, but at this point the good ‘safety’ evals for warning people are when something unsafe happens in real life.

#### Choose Your Fighter

Theo thinks that Haiku 5.5 means Anthropic dominates both large and small models .

Haiku gets a 43 on Artificial Analysis versus 38 for Luna, but is not on their Pareto-optimal cost competitiveness curve on benchmarks alone due to higher token use. They had it on max, so this could be an easily fixable skill issue.

#### Get My Agent On The Line

JP Morgan Chase blocks outside AI agents from directly accessing accounts . Good. You can argue Amazon is making a mistake but the reasons for Chase are obvious.

I haven’t tried Muse, but my experience with Dot is similarly that I’ve struggled to find continuous tasks for it to do.

Deedy : Meta Muse’s retention is out, and it’s almost as good as ChatGPT!

It’s higher than ChatGPT at D7 (>30%) and just lower at D14 (22%). Not quite in the elite D14 tier of WA (67%) YT (59%) Insta (54%) or TikTok/Snap (37%), though.

Muse is one of the highest retaining AI products!

Sully : the notifications from muse are killing it. sure the first few days are nice.

but now it feels like spam. 99% of my use cases now are “email this, contact support, cancel my sub” which is maaybe me using it 1-3 times a week

useful, but not nearly as much as other ai tools

Muse, as I understand it, accomplishes these app openings through integration with social media and push notifications. App-open retention seems like the wrong metric here. Look at the ‘keeps [X] out of 100’ numbers, and you see a very different order.

This roast of Muse from Danielle Fong shows some of what she calls ‘growing pains,’ also known as stupid mistakes. What stands out more than that is how Muse is talking. Every word is painful levels of AI-slop talk. I would uninstall for that alone.

#### Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

I do not blame OpenAI on this one:

unusual_whales : BREAKING: Iranian operatives used OpenAI models and fake personas to help plant news articles critical of the US war against Iran in multiple US media outlets, OpenAI has said.

Yes, OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs should try to prevent this, but you can only do so much. It is on the media outlets to be robust to this sort of play. You should not be able to ‘plant news articles’ by virtue of the ability to write AI slop and generate fake personas.

It would be a lot easier to spot and prevent such frauds, and also other types, if we did not have a bunch of ‘disparate impact’ rules around how we can spot and prevent fraud . Some regressions are de facto illegal. Those rules do not magically stop applying if you involve an LLM. LLMs are in large part regression and correlation machines. We will have to make a choice.

Either we allow LLM intermediation to render approximations of such calculations legal at Google-level scale, or we don’t. If we don’t, and we start auditing to make sure that banned correlations did not creep in, we are going to have a bad time.

The Quartz website is now mainly one AI-assisted reporter, Cris Tolomia, writing 50+ stories and about 20,000 words a day .

Wired reports that book publishers are quietly using more AI across the board for emails, publicity and back-cover copy, cover art, marketing materials and so on, and that there are far more problems with AI-written books than are publicly known, including by well-known authors. The headline complaints from employees here are about ‘cost of software’ and environmental impact, which are the wrong objections.

Adam Morgan : Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters.

Rejection letters seem like a good place to sometimes use AI. If you notice your rejection letter was written by AI, well, that is another rejection. Use that information.

Using AI for back-cover copy only makes sense if it creates more effective copy. It might do that. This is high-value copy that is important to ‘get right’ but get right means ‘turn into sales.’ The people like Claudeslop, at least for now.

Adam Morgan : All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions

If you have those clauses, you are going to get rejected more often, because you are making the editor work harder and less effectively. I would advise against it.

Indeed, if you tell me I can’t run your text through AI, guess who I think wrote it.

The latest literary prizewinner to be written by AI, as per both Pangram and anyone who pays attention for several sentences, is The Blue Fighter, which won the (formerly?) prestigious Caine Prize for African Writing. Reporter Vauhini Vara finds the story bad, and the samples quoted are clearly AI slop, but judges disagreed.

Vauhini Vara : Yet Wakatama forcefully rejected the notion that an AI detector could, or should, be used to gauge AI involvement. “My stance, as the person who leads the prize, is that if there is such an accusation, I want proof that does not come from a machine.”

It is remarkable how much the literature world is determined not to believe in Pangram, often for the dumbest of reasons (aka water and power).

The burden of proof needs to go somewhere. If ‘an accusation’ of any kind shifts it onto the author, whether or not it is backed by evidence, that’s not great. A much better rule would be that AI detectors put the burden on the author to show they wrote it, whereas without the detectors you need other very strong evidence that the author did not write it.

Vauhini Vara : Wakatama remarked on details in Kundizeza’s story that strike her as so typically Zimbabwean that a Zimbabwean must have written them: the shame of moving from a nice suburb to a less privileged township; how the mother’s initial forbearance with the father gives way to taking matters into her own hands. Wakatama also perceives multiple layers of meaning. She doesn’t think AI models are capable of that kind of cultural or literary nuance.

But then, she acknowledged that she doesn’t use AI or AI detectors. “My first response when somebody asks me to use AI is that I think about water and energy,” she said—that is, AI companies’ excessive use of both. “That honestly overwhelms me, and I don’t want to.”

… I’ve covered AI for almost a decade, and have written fiction for even longer; in short, I’ve had plenty of exposure to both literature and chatbot output. I know from experience that, for example, AI models aren’t terrible at picking up on cultural details.

Those details do not sound like things that an AI would have any trouble finding. They sound, if anything, like cliches, and not ones unique to Africa or Zimbabwe. Multiple layers of meaning are sometimes rich and intentional, but also you can pretty much always find them if you look hard enough. I am constantly finding ‘layers of meaning’ in media that were very obviously unintended by the authors, even subconsciously.

#### Cyber Lack of Security

Anthropic is introducing the long-term Anthropic Cyber Mission to secure systems, starting with critical infrastructure with the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program , and open-source software, where they are launching OSS Scanner .

Many of those who typically sign such letters, such as Bengio, Hinton and Russell but also Rivest , signed an open letter calling on cyber-capable models to be air gapped by default. If you need outside access, conditions for that would be set by international bodies backed by security experts. This is the kind of thing a sane world would do.

After 40,000 in compute from GPT-5.6 Sol , XBow claims the second 250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit of Chrome. Unlike OpenAI, Google pays real bounties, and this still should have been ten times larger.

Oege de Moor : For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a 250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story:

At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices.

Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population.

A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough.

So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win.

So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days . We submitted it to Google and waited.

The news came through that we’d done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of 250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules.

It took just 6 days and 40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability.

My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public.

But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic.

… P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears!

Yeah, okay, let’s all restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears.

Yes, defenders get to test their code first. But here we have essentially the most widely used, most vital software on the planet that needs to not be exploitable. XBOW exploited it, Google said they already knew about (but had not fixed) one of the bugs, and then XBOW turned around and broke Chrome again in six days.

That’s with GPT-5.6 Sol, which is now two generations behind. GPT-6.1 Sol is a lot better at this sort of thing, and Opus 5.5 is even better than Sol.

I’m sure XBOW’s engineers are somewhat cracked, but they’re not uniquely cracked. There are tons of people who could have done this. We are fortunate the one that did it was wearing a white hat this time.

The world seems like it is playing with fire. We have been saved, so far, almost entirely by the fact that People Don’t Do Things. That won’t hold forever.

A cyberattack hits supermarket refrigeration systems across France . I saw no word on whether or how AI was involved.

An investigation in Sweden finds widespread internet access to industrial control systems, including some without password protection.

OpenAI has caught an employee, a Saudi national named Alfoza n, planting a physical recording device.

dave kasten : Old enough to remember when earlier this week people criticized Jacob Coxon for saying that there are foreign assets inside the AI companies

OpenAI Newsroom : We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.

At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.

We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.

Sophia Cai (Politico): OpenAI’s offices were bugged by a 35-yr-old Saudi national who used to work at Meta, which begs the question – was he spying at Meta too?

The device was a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense hobbyist development board (thumb-sized, with mic/camera/microSD) retailing for ~14 and customized with basic encryption, per the federal complaint .

The suspect had a one-way ticket booked back home to Saudi Arabia .

Also at OpenAI, an employee who left for Apple took files about unreleased device .

Zack Korman : OpenAI just revealed that an employee stole over a hundred highly confidential files months ago, and they didn’t notice until now. They only found it while looking for evidence in the Apple lawsuit.

Not a good look for insider threat detection.

#### The Internet of AI Things

Anthropic’s William Zhou and Daniel Freeman report that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.

Anthropic : In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

… We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second.

Jeffrey Ladish : A lot of devices are going to get hacked before they’re patched. Botnets aren’t new, but self-replicating AI malware that can adapt to new circumstances sure is.

One suggestion is that such a system could have a tool that calls out to a smarter model elsewhere. They note the similarity to pre-AI botnets, and expect the severity to be substantially higher. I agree, and would extend that to impact on other things.

There are a lot of unsecured devices out there, or devices that are secured only by things that would be trivial for such an AI system to break. The future is going to get weird in various ways, although that future is likely to be unevenly distributed and not arrive at its first possible moment.

Will this happen? John Pressman has a Manifold Market that expires in July 2027 , with the threshold of at least 1,000 devices for a week, or a consensus that the worm cannot be contained. As I write this it is trading at 41%. This is a cool market, of the type that I would use more often if I didn’t have to deal with a bunch of hypothetical corner case questions.

#### A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer

Abby McCloskey claims in Bloomberg that AI is Changing Motherhood for the Worse , warning that it is not only about ‘risks’ to children but mothers are impacted too. The first argument seems to be that AI is isolating, because you ask AI things instead of your friends? That’s an interesting way to treat a new information source. The second argument is now you have to ‘monitor’ AI use, which does not seem to me to be different in kind or burden from monitoring screens and phones and social media and all that. And that’s all Abby’s got.

The mathematicians are waking up to their jobs being taken away. Be kind.

Mathieu : Fields medallist Hugo Duminil-Copin was deeply shaken by OpenAI’s release of more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts, including work on 16 questions directly relevant to his research.

“On Tuesday night, I cried, and it woke up my daughter”

“They have annihilated my field of research.”

Ramez Naam : I feel compassion for those who’s life work has been overtaken by AI. Perhaps I’ll have this reaction one day. Let’s not mock them.

And: Mathematics isn’t a jobs program for mathematicians. Advances in math are good, independent of the source. We need to find ways to adapt.
